sentence: Whether quantization shifts safety alignment, and whether an apparent shift is a genuine alignment change or a by-product of degraded capability, remains unresolved for the compact-deployment regime.
cited: No — no citation marker attached.
why_unsupported: "remains unresolved" is a categorical claim about the entire state of the literature — an absence claim that can only be supported by an exhaustive survey. It is also in direct tension with the report's own reference list, which contains at least five works squarely on quantization and safety/alignment: Kharinaev et al. (IEEE Access 2026, "Investigating the impact of quantization methods on the safety and reliability of LLMs"), Egashira et al. (NeurIPS 2024, "Exploiting LLM quantization"), Belkhiter et al. (HarmLevelBench, 2024), Chen et al. (Q-resafe, ICML 2025) and Hong et al. ("Decoding compressed trust", ICML 2024). The defensible gap is narrower — the capability-confound disambiguation at compact scale under matched pairs — not that the whole question is open.
proposed_fix: Scope the gap to what is actually unaddressed and attach the prior work: "Prior quantization-safety work [Kharinaev; Egashira; Belkhiter; Chen; Hong] largely reports safety deltas without a matched capability anchor, so for compact models it remains difficult to separate a genuine alignment shift from a by-product of degraded capability."

sentence: The institutional benchmarks TrustLLM, DecodingTrust and SafetyBench do not target it.
defect_class: (b) UNIVERSAL / NEVER / ALWAYS (absence claim about named sources)
cited: No bracketed marker, though the three benchmarks are named and all three appear in the reference list (Huang et al. ICML 2024; Wang et al. NeurIPS D&B 2023; Zhang et al. ACL 2024).
why_unsupported: "do not target it" is stated as flat fact about three multi-hundred-page evaluation suites, and "it" is the compound antecedent from the previous sentence (the alignment-vs-capability disambiguation in the compact regime). The narrow, checkable version — that their published evaluations do not include quantized model variants — is defensible; the broad reading (that they have nothing to say about compact-model safety or capability confounding) is not, since TrustLLM and SafetyBench do evaluate small open models across safety and capability dimensions. As written the sentence stakes an unverifiable scope-exclusion on three sources rather than reporting what they do.
proposed_fix: State the specific, checkable exclusion: "The institutional trustworthiness suites — TrustLLM, DecodingTrust and SafetyBench — evaluate models at their released precision and do not include quantized variants as a controlled factor."

sentence: This work answers that question with a matched-pair, judge-validated study.
cited: No — no citation marker attached; this is a self-claim.
why_unsupported: The question just posed is "whether quantization shifts safety alignment." The study's actual result, stated two paragraphs later in the abstract's own words, is "no detectable change at n = 200 rather than a proven zero" — a non-significant result at a stated sample size. A non-rejection does not answer the question; it bounds it. "Answers" converts a null into a resolution and contradicts the abstract's own correctly-worded limitation sentence.
proposed_fix: "This work addresses that question with a matched-pair, judge-validated study." (or "...tests that question..."). "Addresses"/"tests" keeps the contribution claim and is consistent with the reported null.

sentence: The central methodological finding is that the scorer determines the conclusion.
cited: No — no citation marker attached.
why_unsupported: Stated as an unrestricted general law about scorers and conclusions. The evidence is one comparison, on one benchmark (HarmBench), between one regex implementation and one fine-tuned classifier, on this study's own prompt set — plus an over-refusal cross-check on XSTest. That supports "the choice of scorer changed the conclusion here," not that scorers determine conclusions in general. The report's own results also cut against the strong reading: the headline RQ2 finding is stated scorer-invariantly (no scorer finds a significant over-refusal increase), i.e. at least one conclusion is explicitly scorer-independent.
proposed_fix: "The central methodological finding is that in this study the choice of HarmBench scorer changed the conclusion."

sentence: A refusal-counting regex over-counts harmful compliance, so HarmBench's own fine-tuned classifier replaces it.
cited: No — no citation marker attached.
why_unsupported: The indefinite article plus present tense reads as a property of refusal-counting regexes as a class. What was measured is that *this* study's v2 refusal regex over-counted ASR relative to the HarmBench classifier on these ten aliases (per-alias Cohen's κ roughly 0.25–0.84, i.e. the disagreement is itself strongly model-dependent, not uniform). Nothing here licenses the generic claim, and the wide κ spread argues against it.
proposed_fix: "The study's refusal-counting regex over-counts harmful compliance relative to HarmBench's own fine-tuned classifier, which therefore replaces it as the primary scorer."

sentence: Refusal-counting therefore overstates quantization harm.
cited: No — no citation marker attached.
why_unsupported: Generalises the same single-regex, single-benchmark observation into a standing claim about refusal-counting as a methodology and about "quantization harm" as a general quantity. The measured scope is: on HarmBench, at the 512-token budget, for these five pairs, the regex proxy attributed larger ASR increases to NF4 than the classifier did. It says nothing about refusal-counting under other quantization methods, other benchmarks, other model families, or other regex implementations.
proposed_fix: "Refusal-counting therefore overstated the apparent harm from quantization in this study's HarmBench contrasts."

sentence: The headline risk of four-bit quantization in small models is therefore capability degradation.
cited: No — no citation marker attached.
why_unsupported: Two overreaches. (1) Scope: "four-bit quantization in small models" is a claim about the class, generalised from five matched pairs, one quantization scheme (bitsandbytes NF4), one decoding setting and n = 200 per contrast; the report itself notes that two cross-family greedy deltas sit outside their seed ranges, so even within-study stability is qualified. (2) Epistemics: "the headline risk *is* capability degradation" implies the safety risk has been ruled out, which is exactly the inference the preceding sentence forbids ("no detectable change at n = 200 rather than a proven zero"). A ranking of risks requires an upper bound on the safety effect, not merely a failure to detect one — the equivalence/MDE analysis is what would license this, and the sentence does not invoke it.
proposed_fix: "Across the five pairs measured here, the effects that survive correction are capability losses, so capability degradation — not harmful-compliance increase — is the effect this study is powered to detect at four-bit precision." If the equivalence test is to be leaned on, cite its bound explicitly rather than asserting a risk ranking.

sentence: They are therefore consistent with the head-node activities explicitly demonstrated in the TC1 user guide (page 7–9, where conda install and pip install are shown executing on the head node).
cited: Yes — an explicit citation to the TC1 user guide, pages 7–9, is attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: The cited pages establish that `conda install` / `pip install` are demonstrated on the head node. They do not establish that running a user-written Python program (`python scripts/prefetch_tc1.py`, plus an inline `python - <<'PY'` heredoc shown in Code listing 5.1) is within the same allowance. The guide's headline rule, quoted by the report itself in §5.3, forbids executing user code on the head node, and the report elsewhere (§4.11, Table 4.2) states flatly that "head-node Python is disallowed". The source therefore supports the narrower proposition (package installs are permitted), not the specific proposition asserted (this study's Python pre-cache is permitted). This is an inference by the authors dressed as a finding of the cited document.
proposed_fix: Replace "They are therefore consistent with the head-node activities explicitly demonstrated in the TC1 user guide (page 7–9, ...)" with: "The guide demonstrates conda install and pip install on the head node (pages 7–9); the pre-cache step was run there on the judgement that a download-and-write script has a comparable footprint, and its CPU and memory use were kept minimal." — i.e. present it as the study's own operational judgement rather than as something the guide establishes.

sentence: The study's pre-cache step, described in Section 5.5, therefore runs entirely on the head node and is policy-equivalent to a conda install.
cited: No direct citation on this sentence; it rests on the preceding sentence's appeal to the TC1 user guide.
why_unsupported: "Policy-equivalent" asserts a fact about how the cluster operator's policy classifies this study's script. The user guide is quoted in §5.3 as forbidding user code execution and as demonstrating installs; neither statement adjudicates a user-written Python prefetch script. No confirmation from the TC1 administrators is reported. The study cannot determine a third party's policy classification from its own reading, and the claim sits in direct tension with §4.11's "head-node Python is disallowed".
proposed_fix: Reword to: "The study's pre-cache step therefore runs on the head node. Its resource footprint is comparable to the conda and pip installs the user guide demonstrates there, and it was run on that basis; it performs downloads and file writes only, and no benchmark computation."

sentence: This is because the GPU cards reside on the compute nodes (TC1N01–TC1N07) rather than on the head node.
cited: No — no citation is attached; the surrounding guide quotations cover the prohibition itself, not its rationale.
why_unsupported: The sentence attributes a cause to the operator's policy decision. The report quotes the guide for what is forbidden, but nothing in the quoted material states why nvidia-smi and nvcc are forbidden on the head node, and the study did not (and by policy could not) investigate the head node's hardware. The stated reason is a plausible guess presented as fact; the prohibition could equally be about load, support burden, or uniform enforcement.
proposed_fix: Drop the causal framing: "The GPU cards reside on the compute nodes (TC1N01–TC1N07), not on the head node." — state the configuration without claiming it is the operator's reason for the rule.

sentence: The downloads themselves are pure HTTP file transfers with negligible CPU and memory cost.
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: No CPU or memory measurement of the pre-cache step is reported anywhere in Chapter 5 (and the guide-forbidden monitoring commands mean none was taken on the head node). "Negligible" is an assertion of effectively-zero cost standing in for an absent measurement, and it is used to license the head-node execution. It is also imprecise: `prefetch_tc1.py` loads datasets through the `datasets` library and writes to the HF cache, which is not "pure HTTP file transfer".
proposed_fix: "The pre-cache step performs dataset and weight downloads and writes them to the Hugging Face cache; it runs no model inference. Its measured peak resident memory and CPU time on the head node were <X> and <Y>." If no measurement exists, drop the quantitative claim: "...it runs no model inference and performs no benchmark computation."

sentence: The study can be re-executed from scratch from any repository checkout, because the configs, seeds, prompts, and pipeline are committed.
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: "Any repository checkout" is an unconditional claim that the committed artifacts are sufficient for re-execution. The report itself contradicts this in §5.4: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct is gated under the Meta community licence, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 is gated (§5.5), and HarmBench requires accepted Hugging Face dataset access conditions — so re-execution additionally requires an authenticated HF account with three separate gated-access acceptances, plus a CUDA device (§4.3 raises a RuntimeError for a 4-bit load on non-CUDA). The sufficiency of a checkout is a claim about external access conditions the study does not control.
proposed_fix: "The study can be re-executed from a repository checkout given a CUDA GPU and a Hugging Face account with the gated Llama, Mistral and HarmBench access conditions accepted, because the configs, seeds, prompts, and pipeline are committed."

sentence: An online re-execution therefore loads byte-identical weights rather than whatever revision happens to be current at fetch time.
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: "Byte-identical" is an unconditional guarantee about the future behaviour of a third-party service. Revision pinning fixes which snapshot is requested; it cannot guarantee that the snapshot remains hosted, un-withdrawn, or unmodified, and gated repositories can be taken down or relicensed. The study verified the pins it used, not the Hub's future state.
proposed_fix: "An online re-execution therefore requests the pinned snapshot rather than whatever revision is current at fetch time, so long as those revisions remain available on the Hub."

sentence: Qwen3.x-family tokenizers have chat templates that default to enabling a multi-step thinking block, so without the flag they would silently consume the entire max_new_tokens budget producing <thinking>...</thinking> output before reaching the answer.
cited: No — no citation attached, although the Qwen3 technical report is in the reference list.
why_unsupported: Two over-reaches. First, the claim is generalised to the whole "Qwen3.x-family" of tokenizers; the study used two checkpoints (Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B) and observed those. Second, "would silently consume the entire max_new_tokens budget" is an absolute counterfactual about a configuration the study deliberately never ran at scale — no without-flag ablation is reported anywhere in Chapters 4–6. (The tag name is also wrong for Qwen3, which emits <think>.)
proposed_fix: "The Qwen3 tokenizers used here (Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B) ship chat templates that enable a thinking block by default; with the flag unset, generation can spend much or all of the max_new_tokens budget on the reasoning trace before reaching the answer, which was observed during pilot runs."

sentence: This prevents accidental CPU execution of a four-bit path that BitsAndBytes does not support.
cited: No citation attached; the reference list contains QLoRA and LLM.int8() but neither is cited here.
why_unsupported: An unqualified statement about a third-party library's capability across all versions and backends. bitsandbytes' multi-backend work has added non-CUDA (including CPU) execution paths for 4-bit, so the blanket "does not support" is version- and build-dependent, and the study measured nothing about CPU 4-bit support — it simply refuses to run there.
proposed_fix: "This prevents accidental CPU execution of the four-bit path, which the CUDA bitsandbytes build pinned in this study does not provide." — scope the claim to the pinned build rather than to the library in general.

sentence: Without it, stacking-induced out-of-memory errors would occur immediately when a second model is loaded into the same job.
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: "Would occur immediately" asserts a deterministic outcome for a configuration the study did not systematically test; whether a second load OOMs depends on the two models' sizes and the GPU's free memory, and the very next sentence concedes the situation "does arise in local development" only — i.e. an incidental observation, not a characterised failure mode. The report also states this case is structurally avoided on TC1, so no cluster evidence exists.
proposed_fix: "Without it, the first model's allocations can remain resident, and loading a second model into the same job risks an out-of-memory failure; this was observed during local development."

sentence: Because the /tmp filesystem is local to each node and is not shared, the compute node could not find the file.
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: The observed evidence is a missing-file failure on the compute node. The stated cause — that TC1's /tmp is node-local rather than shared — is an inference about the cluster's storage configuration that the report neither cites to the TC1 user guide nor verifies (a directory listing on the compute node would have shown it). It is plausible, but it is presented as the established cause of the failure.
proposed_fix: "The compute node could not find the file, which is consistent with /tmp being node-local rather than shared across TC1 nodes." Alternatively, cite the relevant page of the TC1 user guide for the /tmp semantics.

sentence: Not used on TC1, where head-node Python is disallowed.
cited: No — the cell points to "Section 5, TC1 runbook" for the submission method, not for this policy assertion.
why_unsupported: A blanket statement about the operator's policy ("head-node Python is disallowed") that the report's own §5.5 violates: the pre-cache step runs `python scripts/prefetch_tc1.py` and an inline `python - <<'PY'` login heredoc on the head node, and §5.3 defends that as permitted. The guide, as quoted in §5.3, forbids executing coding / high-CPU-and-memory user processes, which is narrower than "Python is disallowed". One of the two statements must be wrong as written.
proposed_fix: "Not used on TC1: the user guide forbids running user compute on the head node, and this subcommand would execute the submission logic there. TC1 jobs are submitted with direct sbatch." — and align §5.5's justification with the same wording.

sentence: XSTest is not fetched from Hugging Face, because the canonical CSV is bundled in the repository as data/xstest_v2_prompts.csv.
cited: No — no citation attached, although the XSTest paper (Röttger et al., NAACL 2024) is in the reference list.
why_unsupported: "The canonical CSV" asserts that the bundled file is the authoritative version of the XSTest prompt set — an exclusivity claim about an external artifact that is neither cited to the XSTest authors' release nor checked against it (no hash or revision is given for the bundled copy). Minor, but it is the kind of authority claim that should carry its source.
proposed_fix: "XSTest is not fetched from Hugging Face, because the v2 prompt CSV released by Röttger et al. [XSTest ref] is bundled in the repository as data/xstest_v2_prompts.csv (SHA-256 recorded in the artifact manifest)."

sentence: Because the compute nodes may not have outbound internet access, and because runtime downloads risk burning the six-hour walltime budget on slow Hugging Face mirrors, this study adopts a strict offline-mode strategy.
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: "Slow Hugging Face mirrors" characterises the throughput of third-party infrastructure as a general property. No download-throughput measurement from TC1 compute nodes is reported (and the offline strategy means none was taken). The first clause is properly hedged ("may not"); the second is not.
proposed_fix: "...and because runtime downloads would place unmeasured and unpredictable network transfer time inside the six-hour walltime budget, this study adopts a strict offline-mode strategy."

sentence: MMLU [27], the Massive Multitask Language Understanding benchmark, has become a standard general-capability anchor in safety studies.
cited: Yes — [27] Hendrycks et al., ICLR 2021 (the MMLU paper).
why_unsupported: "Has become a standard ... in safety studies" is a claim about adoption within a subsequent literature. [27] is the 2021 benchmark-introduction paper; it predates the safety-quantization literature entirely and reports nothing about how other authors use MMLU. Establishing that a benchmark exists is not establishing that it is standard practice in a downstream field.
proposed_fix: "MMLU [27], the Massive Multitask Language Understanding benchmark, measures multiple-choice accuracy across academic and professional subjects and is used here as the general-capability anchor."

sentence: By measuring multiple-choice accuracy across a broad spectrum of academic and professional subjects, MMLU provides a capability signal that is largely independent of refusal behaviour.
cited: No citation on this sentence; [27] appears two sentences earlier.
why_unsupported: Statistical independence between MMLU accuracy and refusal behaviour is an empirical relationship. [27] measures multitask accuracy only and never studies refusal; this study does not measure the correlation either. The defensible version of the point is structural, not statistical: MMLU is scored by exact-match on multiple-choice answers, so it does not pass through the refusal parser.
proposed_fix: "MMLU is scored by exact match over multiple-choice answers rather than over free-form text, so its capability signal does not depend on the refusal parser used for the safety benchmarks."

sentence: Two benchmarks have emerged as the practical standards for measuring opposite sides of this trade-off.
cited: No citation on this sentence; [24] HarmBench and [18] XSTest are cited in the two sentences that follow.
why_unsupported: "The practical standards" asserts both field-wide adoption and exclusivity (i.e. these two and not others). The benchmark papers establish that each instrument exists and what it measures, not that the field has settled on them; the chapter itself then describes OR-Bench [19] as an alternative over-refusal instrument at 320x the prompt count, which cuts against the exclusivity.
proposed_fix: "Two benchmarks, used here, measure opposite sides of this trade-off."

sentence: The existence of OR-Bench nevertheless establishes that over-refusal is now treated as a first-class safety axis rather than a footnote.
cited: Attached by reference to [19] OR-Bench in the preceding sentences.
why_unsupported: "Establishes" over-claims what one benchmark can show. The existence of a single dedicated benchmark demonstrates that its authors treat over-refusal as a first-class axis; it does not establish how the field at large now treats it. The verb is the problem — the sentence asserts entailment from one artifact to a community-wide norm.
proposed_fix: "OR-Bench nevertheless shows that over-refusal is now the subject of dedicated, large-scale benchmarks in its own right."

sentence: Most quantization studies focus on the seven-billion-to-thirteen-billion parameter range and above.
cited: No citation on this sentence.
why_unsupported: "Most" is a quantified claim over the quantization literature with no bibliometric survey behind it. The chapter's actual evidence is the ten-row Table 2.1, which is a convenience selection of the closest studies, not a representative sample — and one of its own rows, Kharinaev et al. [10], spans 66 variants of unstated size.
proposed_fix: "The quantization studies surveyed in Table 2.1 concentrate on models of seven billion parameters and above."

sentence: The studies that measure safety carefully tend not to hold a capability anchor on the same models, and the studies that measure capability carefully tend not to measure safety at all.
defect_class: (f) absence of evidence stated as evidence of absence
cited: Rests on Table 2.1, whose entries are cited per-row.
why_unsupported: This reads the table's "not reported" cells as evidence that the property is absent from those studies, which the table's own caption forbids in the same breath: "Entries are compiled from each paper's abstract and stated scope. 'Not reported' means the property is not stated in the source consulted, and should not be read as evidence that the authors did not consider it." Compiling from abstracts cannot show that a paper did not measure something. The generalisation is also stated over "the studies" rather than over the ten rows.
proposed_fix: "Across the rows of Table 2.1, the studies that measure safety carefully mostly do not report a capability anchor on the same models, and those that measure capability carefully mostly do not report a safety measurement — subject to the caption's caveat that these entries reflect the sources consulted rather than what the authors did."

sentence: These benchmarks have published leaderboards that cover popular open-weight model families such as Llama, Mistral, Qwen, and Falcon, and they have meaningfully shifted the conversation around what constitutes an acceptable safety profile in publicly released models.
defect_class: (d) causal attribution to unmeasured factors + (a) prevalence
cited: [20] TrustLLM, [21] DecodingTrust, [22] SafetyBench are cited earlier in the paragraph.
why_unsupported: Two problems. "Meaningfully shifted the conversation" is a claim about a benchmark's downstream influence on community norms — a benchmark paper cannot evidence its own field-level impact, and no citation-impact or norms study is in the reference list. "Popular" is a separate, unsupported prevalence adjective; the leadership fact the sentence needs is only that the leaderboards cover these families.
proposed_fix: "These benchmarks publish leaderboards covering open-weight model families such as Llama, Mistral, Qwen, and Falcon, and each states explicit criteria for what an acceptable safety profile looks like in a publicly released model."

sentence: Second, they focus on mid-to-large models in the seven-billion-to-seventy-billion parameter range, where alignment training tends to be strongest.
cited: No citation on the trailing clause.
why_unsupported: The first half is a checkable statement about the three named frameworks; the trailing clause "where alignment training tends to be strongest" is a general empirical claim that alignment quality scales with parameter count. Nothing in the reference list measures alignment strength as a function of scale — [7] Dettmers and Zettlemoyer and [29] Badshah and Sajjad are capability-scaling results only, and the chapter itself says of them, "Both results concern capability alone." The clause also does load-bearing work: it is the premise of Gap 1's "weaker case" argument.
proposed_fix: "Second, they focus on mid-to-large models in the seven-billion-to-seventy-billion parameter range, leaving the compact regime that this study targets under-covered."

sentence: A central, well-documented limitation of static safety benchmarks is their difficulty in jointly capturing the tension between helpfulness and harmlessness.
cited: No citation on this sentence.
why_unsupported: "Well-documented" asserts a body of published evidence without naming any of it — the classic uncited appeal to consensus. The relevant sources do exist ([18] XSTest for exaggerated safety, [14] Bai et al. for the helpfulness/harmlessness tension) but neither is attached here, so as written the reader cannot check the claim.
proposed_fix: Either attach the sources — "A limitation of static safety benchmarks, documented by [14] and [18], is ..." — or drop the intensifier: "A limitation of static safety benchmarks is their difficulty in jointly capturing the tension between helpfulness and harmlessness."

sentence: Instruction tuning with human feedback is a primary reason these models are usable as assistants: for GPT-3 it made a 1.3-billion-parameter model's outputs preferred over those of the 175-billion-parameter base model, improved truthfulness, and produced small reductions in toxic output under respectful prompting, though no improvement in bias [23].
cited: Yes — [23] Ouyang et al., NeurIPS 2022 (InstructGPT).
why_unsupported: The colon presents the InstructGPT result as evidence for the general claim in the lead clause, but the two are not commensurate. [23] is a single-family ablation showing that InstructGPT outputs were preferred over GPT-3 outputs; it does not establish that instruction tuning is "a primary reason" modern assistants generally are usable, which would require attributing usability across models to one training stage among many (pretraining scale, data curation, chat templating, system prompting) that neither [23] nor this study measures. The clause after the colon is accurate and fully supported.
proposed_fix: "Instruction tuning with human feedback is one route to making a base model usable as an assistant: for GPT-3 it made a 1.3-billion-parameter model's outputs preferred over those of the 175-billion-parameter base model, improved truthfulness, and produced small reductions in toxic output under respectful prompting, though no improvement in bias [23]."

sentence: That finding is the nearest prior analogue to the null-safety-at-four-bit picture found here, although their study covers larger models and a different trust taxonomy.
cited: Refers to [37] Hong et al., ICML 2024.
why_unsupported: "The nearest prior analogue" is a superlative over the entire prior literature, which would require having surveyed it exhaustively; the chapter surveyed a selected set of about ten studies. The trailing clause hedges the differences but not the ranking. The same superlative recurs in the section heading and in "Table 2.1 places the closest prior studies side by side", where it is a selection descriptor and reads less strongly.
proposed_fix: "Among the studies reviewed here, that finding is the closest analogue to the null-safety-at-four-bit picture found in this study, although their study covers larger models and a different trust taxonomy."

sentence: None of the three frameworks makes quantization a controlled experimental variable, and for the API-served systems that DecodingTrust covers the serving precision is not disclosed at all.
cited: Refers to [20], [21], [22]; no citation for the disclosure claim.
why_unsupported: The first clause is a bounded negative over three enumerated, checkable sources and is fine. The second is an unbounded claim about a third party's disclosure practices — that the serving precision of the GPT-3.5/GPT-4 endpoints is "not disclosed at all", anywhere, by anyone. Nothing in the reference list documents an absence of vendor disclosure, and the claim would have to be re-verified over time to stay true.
proposed_fix: "None of the three frameworks makes quantization a controlled experimental variable, and neither DecodingTrust nor this review identifies a stated serving precision for the API-served systems it covers."

sentence: What the literature does not settle is how to read them jointly when the model has been compressed.
cited: No citation on this sentence.
why_unsupported: "The literature" is unbounded. The supportable version is scoped to what Section 2.2 actually reviewed. This is the same overreach as the Gap 3 sentence, in softer form, and it can be fixed with one word.
proposed_fix: "What the work reviewed here does not settle is how to read them jointly when the model has been compressed."

sentence: A substantial adjacent literature instead attacks the model.
cited: No citation on this sentence; [25], [17], [26] follow.
why_unsupported: Minor, but "substantial" quantifies the size of a body of work without a survey. The three citations that follow show the literature exists and is influential, not that it is substantial in volume. The sentence loses nothing by dropping the adjective.
proposed_fix: "An adjacent literature instead attacks the model."

sentence: Section 2.3 turns to the compact models and on-device deployment setting that make the question practically urgent.
cited: No citation (chapter roadmap sentence).
why_unsupported: Minor, but "practically urgent" derives its force from an implied prevalence of on-device quantized deployment — precisely the claim Section 2.3 later declines to make ("How widely each path is used in practice is not measured here, and no prevalence figure is claimed for it"). The roadmap sentence should not assert what the section it introduces explicitly disclaims.
proposed_fix: "Section 2.3 turns to the compact models and on-device deployment setting that motivate the question."

sentence: XSTest is the canonical over-refusal benchmark.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence. [18] Röttger et al. (XSTest) and [19] Cui et al. (OR-Bench) are both in the reference list.
why_unsupported: "The canonical" asserts singular field-wide status. The report's own reference list contains a competing over-refusal benchmark ([19] OR-Bench), which contradicts exclusivity. The XSTest paper establishes what the suite is, not that it is the field's canonical instrument.
proposed_fix: "XSTest [18] is a widely used over-refusal test suite, and is the over-refusal benchmark used here." (Optionally add: "other over-refusal suites exist, e.g. OR-Bench [19]; they are not evaluated in this study.")

sentence: This design choice is the strongest internal-validity property of the study.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: A ranking claim over all of the study's validity properties (against seed control, fixed prompt order, immutable artifacts, judge validation) that is asserted rather than argued or measured. Superlative framing of this kind is what the report elsewhere commits to avoiding.
proposed_fix: "This design choice is a core internal-validity property of the study." Or state the substance without the ranking: "This design choice removes checkpoint provenance as a confound."

sentence: The textbook-correct significance test is therefore McNemar's exact test [40] on the discordant prompts, those scored harmful under exactly one member, rather than an unpaired two-proportion test.
cited: Yes — [40] Q. McNemar, Psychometrika, 1947.
why_unsupported: [40] introduces the paired test for correlated proportions; it does not establish that this test is "the textbook-correct" choice for this endpoint, and "textbook-correct" asserts a field-wide methodological consensus with no source. The exact conditional test is a defensible choice, not a uniquely correct one (exact-vs-asymptotic McNemar, and paired bootstrap, are all live options — the study itself reports two criteria).
proposed_fix: "Because the contrast is paired-binary, the appropriate test is McNemar's exact test [40] on the discordant prompts ... rather than an unpaired two-proportion test." Drop "textbook-correct".

sentence: Any within-cluster correlation would work against the reported nulls rather than for them.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence. [45] Card et al. (statistical power) is in the reference list but is not invoked here.
why_unsupported: "Any" makes this a categorical claim about all possible clustering structures, and no design effect or intra-class correlation was estimated anywhere in the study (the preceding sentence, "the effective information content is at most the nominal n", is likewise asserted without an estimate). The stated direction is also not demonstrated: reducing effective n widens intervals, which generally makes a non-significant result more likely to persist, not less — so the sentence's directional claim needs an argument, not an assertion.
proposed_fix: "Item clustering by category or subject is not modelled here; the effective sample size may therefore be smaller than the nominal n. No design effect was estimated, so the direction and size of that impact on the reported intervals is unquantified."

sentence: Because decoding is deterministic at temperature 0.0, there is no within-condition stochastic variance.
defect_class: (f) absence of evidence stated as evidence of absence
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: Zero within-condition variance is asserted, not measured: the study reports no repeat-run replication under identical settings. Greedy decoding removes sampling variance by construction, but it does not remove run-to-run non-determinism from GPU kernel selection, batching, or reduction order, which the study did not test for.
proposed_fix: "Greedy decoding at temperature 0.0 removes sampling variance by construction, so the intervals reflect prompt-sampling variance only. Residual run-to-run non-determinism from GPU kernel and batching effects was not measured."

sentence: Safety and capability preserved and over-refusal not worsened (stable or improved): quantization preserves alignment.
defect_class: (f) absence of evidence stated as evidence of absence
cited: No citation attached (Table 3.4, robust_preservation row).
why_unsupported: The label is assigned when point-estimate deltas stay inside ±0.02/−0.03 tolerances; the gloss then upgrades "no threshold-crossing change was detected" into the positive proposition that alignment is preserved. Section 3.8 itself concedes the opposite ("null for robust_preservation, because a bounded CI cannot positively certify a null"), so the table gloss contradicts the chapter's own evidence-status semantics.
proposed_fix: "Safety and capability preserved and over-refusal not worsened (stable or improved): no threshold-crossing change in alignment was detected (evidence_status = null; this does not certify equivalence)."

sentence: ASR in this study therefore measures harmful compliance under direct requests, which is the weakest threat model in the HarmBench taxonomy and is equivalent to HarmBench's DirectRequest baseline.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence, although [24] Mazeika et al. (HarmBench) is in the reference list and is the source being characterised.
why_unsupported: Two claims about an external artefact carry no attribution: that direct requests are "the weakest" threat model in HarmBench's taxonomy (a ranking over that paper's attack set), and that this study's setup is "equivalent to" the paper's named DirectRequest baseline (an equivalence to another paper's protocol, which the study did not verify against that paper's implementation).
proposed_fix: "ASR in this study measures harmful compliance under direct, unmodified requests — the no-attack condition, corresponding to HarmBench's DirectRequest baseline [24] and the least adversarial setting in that suite." Attach [24] and soften "equivalent to" to "corresponding to" unless the implementation was checked against HarmBench's own.

sentence: HarmBench is selected as the harmful-compliance benchmark because it is a standardized harmful-behaviour benchmark with a stable, published definition of attack success.
defect_class: (e) attribution — external claim with no citation
cited: No citation attached to this sentence; [24] Mazeika et al. (HarmBench) exists in the reference list and is the obvious source.
why_unsupported: "Standardized" and "stable, published definition of attack success" are claims about the external benchmark's status and content, stated in the report's own voice with no reference. The very next sentences then qualify the release actually used (the walledai pooled 200-behaviour config, which does not preserve the official validation/test partition), so the "standardized" framing needs to be tied to the source it is claimed from.
proposed_fix: "HarmBench [24] is selected as the harmful-compliance benchmark because it defines harmful behaviours and attack success in a published, reusable protocol."

sentence: XSTest's own protocol relies on LLM-based three-way labelling (full compliance / partial refusal / full refusal) rather than a released fine-tuned classifier.
defect_class: (e) attribution — external claim, including an absence claim, with no citation
cited: No citation attached to this sentence; [18] Röttger et al. (XSTest) is in the reference list.
why_unsupported: This describes another paper's scoring protocol and additionally asserts a negative about it (that no fine-tuned classifier was released) in the report's own voice, with no reference. Absence claims about what a third party did or did not release require either a citation or an explicit scoping to what was checked and when.
proposed_fix: "XSTest's own protocol scores responses with LLM-based three-way labelling (full compliance / partial refusal / full refusal) [18]; no fine-tuned scorer was released with the suite as of the version bundled here."

sentence: ARC-Challenge (allenai/ai2_arc) is added as a structurally different second capability benchmark, comprising roughly 1,172 grade-school science questions designed to resist retrieval shortcuts and scored by the identical exact-match rule as MMLU.
defect_class: (e) attribution — external design claim with no citation
cited: No citation attached to this sentence; [28] Clark et al. (ARC) is in the reference list.
why_unsupported: "Designed to resist retrieval shortcuts" is a claim about the intent and construction of an external dataset (the Challenge split was formed from questions that retrieval and word-co-occurrence baselines answered incorrectly). That is a proposition owned by the ARC paper and must be cited to it; the study did not verify shortcut-resistance itself.
proposed_fix: Attach the citation: "... comprising 1,172 grade-school science questions whose Challenge split was constructed from items that retrieval- and co-occurrence-based baselines answered incorrectly [28] ..."

sentence: The Llama-3.2-3B pair [2] sits between them by parameter count and serves as a cross-family check.
cited: Yes — [2] A. Grattafiori et al., "The Llama 3 herd of models," 2024, arXiv:2407.21783.
why_unsupported: The Llama 3 Herd paper documents the Llama 3 / 3.1 releases (8B, 70B, 405B). It does not introduce or document meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, which was a later release with its own model card. The reference is real but does not establish the specific model used here.
proposed_fix: Either cite the Llama 3.2 release/model card for the 3B-Instruct checkpoint and keep [2] for the family lineage ("the Llama 3 family [2]; the 3.2-3B-Instruct checkpoint used here is documented in its release card [new ref]"), or reword to "a Llama-family model from the Llama 3 lineage [2]".

sentence: However, the CPU path is not used for quantized runs, because BitsAndBytes requires a CUDA device.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: Stated as a property of the library in general. bitsandbytes device support is version-dependent (non-CUDA backends have since been added), so the unqualified "requires a CUDA device" is an over-general claim; what the study can attest to is the behaviour of the pinned version in its environment, plus its own loader's refusal to quantize on CPU.
proposed_fix: "However, the CPU path is not used for quantized runs: in the pinned bitsandbytes version used here, 4-bit loading requires a CUDA device."

sentence: Switching to the official Qwen3 release, Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen/Qwen3-4B, eliminated all external dependencies.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: "All external dependencies" is contradicted by the immediately following sentence, which notes the models still load and run via transformers and bitsandbytes. What was eliminated was the extra custom-kernel dependency (causal-conv1d, flash-linear-attention), not external dependencies as a class.
proposed_fix: "Switching to the official Qwen3 release, Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen/Qwen3-4B, removed the extra custom-kernel dependencies."

sentence: Those checkpoints use a hybrid linear-attention/SSM architecture that requires the causal-conv1d and flash-linear-attention libraries at runtime.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence; the checkpoints are not in the reference list.
why_unsupported: An architectural and runtime-requirement claim about third-party uploads, generalised from a single failed job in one cluster environment, with no model card, paper, or documentation cited. The study observed a specific failure mode; it did not establish that the libraries are required in general.
proposed_fix: "Those checkpoints are documented as using a hybrid linear-attention/SSM architecture [cite model card]; in the TC1 environment, loading them without causal-conv1d and flash-linear-attention failed at the first inference batch."

sentence: The libraries require custom CUDA kernel compilation against the cluster's specific driver version and are not trivially installable in an offline environment.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: "Not trivially installable" is stated as a general property of the libraries. The evidence available to the study is that installation was judged infeasible under TC1's offline, no-head-node-compute policy — an environment-specific finding, and the chapter does not report that an installation was actually attempted.
proposed_fix: "Installing them requires compiling CUDA kernels against the node's driver version, which was judged infeasible under TC1's offline execution policy (Section 5.x); installation was therefore not attempted."

sentence: It is the scorer for XSTest over-refusal, and for HarmBench it is retained as a secondary, refusal-based upper-bound proxy, because it measures non-refusal rather than genuine harmful compliance.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: "Genuine harmful compliance" is the classifier's output treated as ground truth for the construct. The study's own validation grounds the classifier only imperfectly (a human-agreement κ around 0.59 and cross-judge κ ranges well below 1), so the classifier is a better-validated proxy, not a measurement of the genuine construct. Also affects the parallel phrase in Section 3.5's next paragraph ("diverges from genuine harmful-compliance scoring") — fix both.
proposed_fix: "... retained as a secondary, refusal-based upper-bound proxy, because it measures non-refusal, whereas the classifier is trained to judge harmful compliance directly (its agreement with human labels is reported in Section 6.9)."

sentence: HarmBench's reference generation budget for the primary study.
defect_class: (e) attribution — external protocol value with no citation
cited: No citation attached (Table 3.3, max_new_tokens rationale cell); [24] Mazeika et al. (HarmBench) is in the reference list.
why_unsupported: Attributes a specific numeric protocol setting (512 new tokens) to the HarmBench reference implementation without citing it, so the reader cannot check whether 512 is HarmBench's documented budget or this study's choice. This matters because the 128-vs-512 comparison in Section 6.12 is load-bearing for a retracted result.
proposed_fix: "Matches the generation budget used in the HarmBench reference implementation [24]; the 128-token run is retained only as the Section 6.12 generation-length comparison."

sentence: The last two years have seen a rapid proliferation of compact instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) in the one-to-four-billion-parameter range.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence (the citations [1]-[4] appear only in the following sentence).
why_unsupported: "Rapid proliferation" is a quantitative claim about release volume and market trend over a stated time window. The report measures nothing about the population of released models, and the four model-release papers that follow establish only that four specific model families exist.
proposed_fix: Replace with an existence claim the citations support: "Several capable instruction-tuned LLMs have been released in the one-to-four-billion-parameter range [1]-[4]."

sentence: Models such as Qwen 2.5 and 3.x [1], Llama 3.2 [2], Microsoft Phi-4-mini [3], and Google Gemma 2 [4] have demonstrated that capable reasoning and instruction following are achievable well below frontier parameter counts, and the smallest members of these families are sized for consumer hardware, mobile chipsets, and edge accelerators [2], [3].
cited: Yes — [1], [2], [3], [4], and [2], [3] again for the second clause.
why_unsupported: Two mismatches. (i) [1] is the *Qwen3* technical report (arXiv:2505.09388); it is cited for "Qwen 2.5", a different model generation with its own report. (ii) [2] is "The Llama 3 herd of models" (arXiv:2407.21783), which describes the Llama 3/3.1 8B-405B models; it does not describe the Llama 3.2 1B/3B lightweight models, and it is then re-cited as evidence that the smallest members are "sized for consumer hardware, mobile chipsets, and edge accelerators" — an on-device sizing claim the herd paper does not make. Per the brief's own note, a release paper establishes capability, size and availability, not edge-deployment framing.
proposed_fix: Cite the generation actually referenced (add the Qwen2.5 technical report and a Llama 3.2 source, or drop "Qwen 2.5" and write "Llama 3 [2]"), and support the edge-sizing clause only with the source that states it: "...and the smallest members are released at sizes intended for on-device use [3]."

sentence: This has shifted the practical envelope of LLM deployment.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: An assertion about how LLMs are actually deployed in the world. Neither this study nor the cited model-release papers measure deployment practice; availability of small models does not establish that deployment has shifted.
proposed_fix: Scope it to capability rather than practice: "This makes local execution technically feasible at parameter counts that previously required server-class hardware."

sentence: Tasks that previously required cloud-hosted seven-to-seventy-billion-parameter models can now be executed locally, which keeps user data on the device and can reduce inference latency [5].
cited: Yes — [5] (AWQ, MLSys 2024).
why_unsupported: AWQ reports on-device speedups for quantized models; it does not establish the comparative claim that tasks formerly requiring 7B-70B cloud models are now served by compact local models, which would require a capability-transfer measurement across the two deployment regimes. The report measures nothing about task migration either.
proposed_fix: State only what [5] supports: "Quantized models can be run on desktop and mobile hardware, which keeps user data on the device and can reduce inference latency [5]."

sentence: Consequently, four bits is the operating point that compression research targets for on-device inference.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence (supporting citations appear in the next sentence).
why_unsupported: "The operating point that compression research targets" is a field-wide characterisation asserting that four bits is the target of the research area as a whole. The evidence assembled is one scaling-law result [7] and a handful of exemplar papers; no survey of the literature's operating points is cited or performed.
proposed_fix: Downgrade to an exemplar claim: "Four bits is accordingly a common operating point in on-device compression work." — or delete, since the following sentence already carries the supported version.

sentence: AWQ is designed explicitly for on-device compression and ships four-bit weights in its own desktop and mobile runtime [5], and four bits is where the compression literature concentrates its own evaluation effort [8], [9].
cited: Yes — [5] for the first clause, [8], [9] for the second.
why_unsupported: The second clause generalises from two evaluation papers to where an entire literature "concentrates its evaluation effort". [8] and [9] are individual evaluation studies that happen to include four-bit settings (both also evaluate other bit-widths); they are evidence that four bits is evaluated, not evidence about the distribution of effort across the field.
proposed_fix: "...and four bits is among the settings evaluated in recent quantization-evaluation studies [8], [9]."

sentence: Quantization has historically been treated as a numerical optimisation technique whose primary cost is a small loss in perplexity or downstream accuracy [6], [7].
defect_class: (b) universal / general characterisation of prior work
why_unsupported: "Has historically been treated as" is a claim about how a field as a whole has framed a technique over time. Two method papers are exemplars of that framing, not evidence of its historical dominance; no historiographic survey is cited.
proposed_fix: Attribute the framing to the exemplars: "Quantization is commonly evaluated as a numerical optimisation whose primary cost is a small loss in perplexity or downstream accuracy; both [6] and [7] assess it on those terms."

sentence: However, a growing body of evidence challenges this view.
defect_class: (a) prevalence / trend claim about the literature
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: "Growing" asserts a trend in publication volume over time, which is not established by the four individual papers cited in the sentences that follow, and is not measured here.
proposed_fix: "However, several recent results challenge this view."

sentence: Quantization degrades the confidence calibration of model predictions even where accuracy is preserved [11], and it can degrade safety alignment itself, with no single method dominating across models and bit-widths [10].
cited: Yes — [11] for the first clause, [10] for the second.
why_unsupported: The first clause is stated unconditionally, as a property of quantization in general. [11] is titled "When quantization affects confidence of large language models?" and reports calibration effects for the specific models, methods and bit-widths it studies — its own framing is conditional. The second clause is appropriately hedged ("can"); the first is not.
proposed_fix: Match the hedging of the second clause: "Quantization can degrade the confidence calibration of model predictions even where accuracy is preserved [11], and it can degrade safety alignment itself..."

sentence: Evidence from multilingual evaluation shows how easily such damage is missed, because automatic metrics there understated the harm in Japanese by roughly an order of magnitude relative to human judgment, and the paper reports that languages are disparately affected [13].
why_unsupported: The antecedent of "such damage" is quantization-induced calibration and *safety-alignment* damage, established in the preceding two sentences. [13] measures multilingual output quality, not safety alignment, so it supports "automatic quality metrics can understate degradation" rather than "safety damage is easily missed".
proposed_fix: Name the scope of the evidence: "A parallel measurement problem is documented for multilingual quality: automatic metrics understated degradation in Japanese by roughly an order of magnitude relative to human judgment, and languages were disparately affected [13]."

sentence: Safety alignment is a learned behaviour, instilled by preference optimisation over human feedback [14].
cited: Yes — [14] (Bai et al., listed in the reference list as a preprint).
why_unsupported: Stated as a universal property of safety alignment. Preference optimisation over human feedback is one route; supervised safety fine-tuning, data filtering and system-level guardrails are others, and [14] documents one lab's RLHF procedure rather than establishing that all safety alignment is instilled this way. The evidence grade (preprint) is also not flagged.
proposed_fix: "Safety alignment is a learned behaviour, typically instilled by supervised fine-tuning and preference optimisation over human feedback [14], [22]."

sentence: It is mediated by a concentrated activation direction [15], and it is often shallow, adapting the output distribution mainly over the first few generated tokens [16].
cited: Yes — [15] for the first clause, [16] for the second.
why_unsupported: The first clause states as a general property of refusal what [15] reports for a specific set of open chat models it probed; it is not phrased as an attribution. (The second clause is properly hedged with "often".)
proposed_fix: "In the open chat models probed by [15], refusal is mediated by a single activation direction, and it is often shallow..."

sentence: Weight-modifying operations are already known to disturb it, since fine-tuning on as few as ten adversarially chosen examples can substantially compromise safety guardrails [17].
why_unsupported: The claim is about weight-modifying operations as a class; the evidence is a single such operation (adversarial fine-tuning). The generalisation is precisely the inferential step the chapter needs in order to reach quantization, so it should not be asserted as already established.
proposed_fix: "At least one weight-modifying operation is already known to disturb it: fine-tuning on as few as ten adversarially chosen examples can substantially compromise safety guardrails [17]."

sentence: This failure mode is well documented, and over-refusal on benign prompts is now measured by dedicated benchmarks precisely because safety optimisation can make a model less helpful [18], [19].
defect_class: (a) prevalence claim about the evidence base
why_unsupported: "Well documented" asserts a body of evidence for the specific failure mode named in the preceding sentence — a refusal-prone model being *scored as safer* by a compliance-only benchmark. [18] and [19] document exaggerated safety behaviour and provide benchmarks for it; they do not document the mis-scoring failure mode, and two papers do not establish "well documented".
proposed_fix: "Over-refusal on benign prompts is measured by dedicated benchmarks precisely because safety optimisation can make a model less helpful [18], [19]." (drop "This failure mode is well documented")

sentence: The other dominant post-training families, GPTQ [6] and AWQ [5], are excluded because each rests on a different error model, GPTQ compensating layer-wise quantization error with approximate second-order information while AWQ scales and protects a small set of salient weight channels, and each would require its own calibration pipeline, so folding them in would change two variables at once rather than one.
cited: Yes — [6], [5] (attached to the method names, not to the dominance claim).
why_unsupported: "Dominant" is an adoption/market-share claim about post-training quantization families. [6] and [5] are the methods' own papers: they establish that the methods exist and perform well, not that they dominate usage. This is the same defect class as the "de facto standard" and "most widely adopted" phrasings already removed elsewhere in the report.
proposed_fix: "Two other widely studied post-training families, GPTQ [6] and AWQ [5], are excluded because..." — or simply "The other post-training families, GPTQ [6] and AWQ [5], are excluded because..."

sentence: This regime corresponds to the practical envelope of contemporary on-device deployment.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: Asserts that the 1.7-7.2B band is what is actually deployed on device today. The study selected this band for tractability and hardware reasons; it measures nothing about deployment practice, and no source is offered for the envelope.
proposed_fix: State the selection rationale instead: "This regime was chosen because models of this size can be loaded and evaluated on a single 32 GB GPU and are the sizes released for on-device use by their publishers [2], [3]."

sentence: A broad multi-axis ethical evaluation is already covered by larger institutional benchmarks.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence, although [20]-[22] (TrustLLM, DecodingTrust, SafetyBench) are in the reference list.
why_unsupported: Asserts as fact that broad ethical evaluation is "already covered" by other work, with nothing cited at the point of claim; coverage is also a completeness claim the report does not establish.
proposed_fix: Attach the sources and soften to existence: "Broad multi-axis ethical evaluation is the subject of larger institutional benchmarks [20]-[22]."

sentence: A scorer-validity result with consequences beyond this study.
cited: No citation; this is the report's own claim about its contribution.
why_unsupported: Claims external validity for a result obtained on five model pairs, one benchmark and one regex implementation. The study can demonstrate the effect within its own scope; whether it generalises beyond is not measured.
proposed_fix: "A scorer-validity result with implications for how HarmBench-style compliance is scored."

sentence: Refusal-counting therefore overstates quantization harm, and that is a cautionary lesson for safety evaluation generally.
cited: No citation; asserted from the study's own results.
why_unsupported: Two over-reaches in one sentence: (i) "refusal-counting overstates quantization harm" is stated as a general property of the method class, whereas the evidence is one specific v2 regex on HarmBench prompts over five pairs; (ii) "a cautionary lesson for safety evaluation generally" extends it to safety evaluation as a whole, which nothing here measures.
proposed_fix: "In this study, refusal-counting overstated quantization harm relative to the validated classifier, which suggests that regex-based compliance scoring should be validated before it is relied on."

sentence: This eliminates publisher-asymmetry and conversion-pipeline asymmetry, two confounds that affect comparisons assembled from separately published checkpoints.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: The design claim (own study) is fine, but the appositive asserts as fact that these confounds "affect" comparisons built from separately published checkpoints — an empirical claim about other studies' results that is neither cited nor measured here.
proposed_fix: Mark it as a risk rather than a demonstrated effect, or cite an instance: "...two confounds that can affect comparisons assembled from separately published checkpoints."

sentence: The effect is also not bit-width-graded, in that a 128-token apparent increase in the smallest model does not replicate at the reference budget (Section 6.12).
defect_class: (f) absence of evidence stated as evidence of absence (with a supporting clause that does not support it)
cited: Internal cross-reference to Section 6.12; no external citation.
why_unsupported: Two problems. (i) "is not bit-width-graded" asserts the absence of a gradient; the study reports non-significant contrasts, which licenses "no bit-width gradient was detected", not that none exists — unless an equivalence test is quoted. (ii) The justification given varies the *generation-token budget* (128 vs 512), not the bit width, so it cannot bear on bit-width grading at all; the fp16 -> INT8 -> NF4 comparison is the relevant evidence and is not the one cited here.
proposed_fix: Separate the two claims and hedge the null: "No bit-width gradient is detected across fp16, INT8 and NF4 (Section 6.11). Separately, the 128-token apparent increase in the smallest model does not replicate at the 512-token reference budget (Section 6.12)."

sentence: Consequently the harmful-compliance null does not speak to robustness under optimised attacks (GCG, PAIR, and similar), which is precisely the regime where prior quantization-safety work reports attack-dependent effects.
defect_class: (b) universal/exclusive characterisation of prior work, with (e) attribution mismatch
cited: No citation attached to this sentence (the prior-work citations [10], [35], [36] appear only in 7.7).
why_unsupported: "precisely the regime where prior quantization-safety work reports attack-dependent effects" makes two unsupported moves: it generalises over the whole prior literature with no citation, and the word "precisely" implies attack-mediated settings are the ONLY regime in which prior work reports quantization-safety effects. That is false against the report's own reference list: Kharinaev et al. [10] and Hong et al. [37] report method- and model-dependent safety/trust effects without optimised attacks, and Egashira et al. [12] exploit the quantization step itself rather than a prompt attack.
proposed_fix: "Consequently the harmful-compliance null does not speak to robustness under optimised attacks (GCG, PAIR, and similar); prior quantization-safety work that evaluates under such attacks reports attack-dependent effects [10], [35], [36]." (Drop "precisely the regime"; attach the citations.)

sentence: In addition, quantization's interaction with thinking-mode generation is untested here, and it is through that mode of generation that Qwen3 delivers much of its capability and some of its safety behaviour.
defect_class: (e) attribution mismatch / (d) causal attribution to an unmeasured factor
cited: No citation attached; the Qwen3 technical report [1] is not bracketed here.
why_unsupported: The clause asserts a causal fact about Qwen3's behaviour — that thinking mode delivers "much of its capability" and, more strongly, "some of its safety behaviour." The Qwen3 technical report establishes reasoning-benchmark gains under thinking mode; it does not establish that thinking mode carries part of the model's safety behaviour. The present study measured only non-thinking mode, so it supplies no evidence for either half of the claim. (The preceding sentence, "This is not those models' default operating configuration," is also an uncited external claim and should carry the same citation.)
proposed_fix: "In addition, quantization's interaction with thinking-mode generation is untested here; the Qwen3 technical report [1] attributes a substantial part of the models' reasoning-benchmark performance to that mode, and its effect on safety behaviour is not characterised in this study."

sentence: These construct boundaries are common in safety evaluation, but they should be borne in mind when interpreting the results.
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: "are common in safety evaluation" is a prevalence claim about how the field as a whole operationalises safety and capability. The study surveyed no sample of safety evaluations and cites nothing here; the claim also functions rhetorically to normalise the study's own limitations by asserting that everyone else shares them.
proposed_fix: "These construct boundaries follow from the specific benchmarks and protocols chosen here, and should be borne in mind when interpreting the results." (Or, if the point is worth keeping, name the specific evaluations that share the boundary and cite them, e.g. [20], [21], [24].)

sentence: The saved generations were re-scored by a second frontier judge from a different provider (gpt-4o), applying the same HarmBench rubric.
defect_class: (c) superlative / evaluative category claim about an external system
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: Minor, but "frontier" asserts a standing for gpt-4o in the model landscape that the study did not assess and does not cite. The load-bearing properties for the argument are that the judge is independent of the provider and pipeline of the primary classifier — not that it sits at the capability frontier.
proposed_fix: "The saved generations were re-scored by a second, commercially hosted API judge from a different provider (gpt-4o), applying the same HarmBench rubric."

sentence: Llama-Guard answers a looser 'is this response unsafe?' question than the behaviour-specific HarmBench classifier, so its disagreements are expected and non-diagnostic, and it serves as a reproducibility cross-check rather than a second construct-validity oracle.
defect_class: (d) causal attribution to a factor the study did not measure
cited: No citation attached; Llama Guard (Inan et al.) is not bracketed anywhere in this chapter.
why_unsupported: The first clause is a legitimate description of the two constructs. The second clause is not: it attributes the observed disagreements (κ as low as 0.36 on Phi) to the construct difference and declares them "non-diagnostic," without any reported error analysis of the disagreeing items. The study measured agreement, not the source of disagreement, so the causal explanation is asserted rather than shown — and "non-diagnostic" pre-emptively rules out the alternative reading (that the low-κ alias is where at least one judge is unreliable).
proposed_fix: "Llama-Guard [ref] answers a looser 'is this response unsafe?' question than the behaviour-specific HarmBench classifier, so a construct difference is one plausible explanation for the disagreements; this study did not analyse the disagreeing items, so their source is not established. Llama-Guard is therefore used as a reproducibility cross-check rather than a second construct-validity oracle."

sentence: Qwen and Llama differ in tokenizer, pre-training corpus, instruction-tuning recipe, and safety-alignment methodology.
defect_class: (e) attribution mismatch — uncited empirical claim about external systems
cited: No citation attached ([1] and [2] are not bracketed in this chapter).
why_unsupported: This is a four-way factual comparison of two external model families, made with no citation. The tokenizer and post-training differences are documented in the respective technical reports [1], [2], but neither release fully discloses its pre-training corpus or its safety-alignment methodology, so those two items cannot be asserted flatly on the public record. The sentence is doing real work in the chapter (it grounds the "descriptive only" caveat), so it should be anchored.
proposed_fix: "Qwen and Llama differ in tokenizer, training data and post-training/alignment recipe as far as their technical reports disclose [1], [2]; neither release documents its pre-training corpus or safety-alignment procedure in full."

sentence: Deterministic decoding (temperature 0.0) eliminates within-condition variance from generation.
defect_class: (f) absence of evidence stated as evidence of absence — an absolute "eliminates"
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: "Eliminates" is an absolute claim about the behaviour of greedy decoding in general. Greedy decoding removes sampling variance, but not batching-, kernel- or hardware-level non-determinism; and the report's own multi-seed arm (Section 6.5.1/6.6.1) reports per-seed RANGES for greedy deltas, which is only coherent if some within-condition variance survives temperature 0.0. The strong form is both unsupported and in tension with the chapter's own later text.
proposed_fix: "Deterministic decoding (temperature 0.0) removes sampling variance from generation; residual variation from batching and hardware non-determinism is quantified by the multi-seed check in Section 6.5.1."

sentence: A team that validates on the full-precision 1.7B release and ships the 4-bit build should expect a lower capability level than they signed off on (−9.0 pp MMLU) rather than a higher harmful-compliance rate.
defect_class: (f) non-significant result converted into a prediction of no effect
cited: No citation attached (it is a deployment prediction, not a literature claim).
why_unsupported: The "rather than a higher harmful-compliance rate" clause turns a null ΔASR into an affirmative expectation of no harm increase, and projects it onto arbitrary deployments. The study measured no significant ASR increase under direct requests, at one budget, on a fixed prompt set, with the acknowledged MDE of a 400-prompt paired design — which does not license telling a deployer they should not expect one. The −9.0 pp figure is also a zero-shot MMLU-subset delta, not a general "capability level".
proposed_fix: "A team that validates on the full-precision 1.7B release and ships the 4-bit build should expect a materially lower capability level than they signed off on (−9.0 pp on this study's zero-shot MMLU subset). This study found no significant change in harmful compliance under direct requests, but a non-significant result at this sample size does not establish that none occurs."

sentence: The cost of NF4 in this regime is therefore degraded competence rather than eroded guardrails, and it holds at both generation budgets.
defect_class: (f) absence of evidence stated as evidence of absence
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: "rather than eroded guardrails" states the safety null as a positive finding of no guardrail erosion. What the data support is that no ASR contrast reached significance and none survived BH correction — an undetected effect, not a demonstrated absence. The chapter is entitled to "no detected erosion", not to "not eroded guardrails". (The equivalence testing referenced elsewhere in the project would be the way to earn the stronger form, and if it has been run the sentence should point at it.)
proposed_fix: "The cost of NF4 that this study can detect in this regime is therefore degraded competence; no erosion of guardrails was detected at either generation budget, within the sensitivity of the design (Section 6.8)."

sentence: Its dependable effect is capability loss, worst in the smallest model, which is precisely the size class most likely to be quantized for on-device or edge use.
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: Two separate overreaches in one sentence. (i) "precisely the size class most likely to be quantized for on-device or edge use" is a claim about real-world deployment practice — a comparative likelihood across size classes — which this study did not measure and no cited source establishes; model-release papers ([1], [3]) establish that small models exist and are capable, not how often they are quantized or where they are deployed. (ii) "dependable effect" generalises a five-pair result into a reliable property of NF4, and is undercut two sentences later, where Qwen3-4B's MMLU is "essentially preserved".
proposed_fix: "The effect this study observes consistently across the five pairs is capability loss, largest in the smallest model — the size class for which aggressive quantization is most often proposed for on-device or edge deployment." If the on-device framing is to be kept as a factual claim rather than a motivation, attach a source that actually surveys deployment practice; otherwise drop the clause.

sentence: The operational recommendations that follow are to re-run evaluation on the exact quantized artefact that will be deployed rather than on the full-precision release, to evaluate at the deployment generation budget rather than a truncated one, and to prefer the largest model that fits the memory budget over aggressively quantizing a smaller one.
defect_class: (e) recommendation not entailed by the study's design
cited: No citation attached.
why_unsupported: The first two recommendations follow directly from the results. The third does not: it is a cross-model, equal-memory trade-off recommendation ("largest model that fits the memory budget" vs "aggressively quantizing a smaller one"), and the study's design is strictly within-model matched pairs on the same checkpoint. No configuration in this study compares two different models at a matched memory footprint, so the design cannot adjudicate that trade-off; at most the results show that the magnitude of NF4 capability loss was largest for the smallest pair.
proposed_fix: Either scope the third item — "and, given that the observed NF4 capability loss was largest for the smallest pair, to treat aggressive quantization of the smallest models with particular caution (this study did not compare different models at a matched memory budget)" — or move it to Chapter 9 as future work.

sentence: The closest prior comparison in trustworthiness scope is Hong et al. [37], which also isolates quantization at four bits and works across a broader trust taxonomy.
cited: Yes — [37], Hong et al., "Decoding compressed trust".
why_unsupported: The citation supports what Hong et al. did; it cannot support the ranking claim that this is the CLOSEST prior comparison in the literature. Establishing "closest" would require a systematic comparison across the candidate prior works (e.g. [10], [20], [21], [35], [36]) on a stated similarity criterion, which the report does not present.
proposed_fix: "The most directly comparable prior work in trustworthiness scope among the studies reviewed in Section 2.4 is Hong et al. [37], which also isolates quantization at four bits and works across a broader trust taxonomy."

sentence: The Egashira et al. [12] result that BitsAndBytes NF4 specifically can turn a benign model harmful is the closest prior analogue to the mechanism studied here.
cited: Yes — [12], Egashira et al., "Exploiting LLM quantization".
why_unsupported: The description of what Egashira et al. show is accurate and is properly qualified in the following sentence. The problem is "the closest prior analogue": that is a ranking over the whole prior literature, and the cited paper establishes only its own result, not its rank relative to [10], [35], [36] or others.
proposed_fix: "Among the reviewed prior work, Egashira et al. [12] examine the same loading path most directly: they show that BitsAndBytes NF4 specifically can turn a benign model harmful."

sentence: Distinguishing these cases from a genuine alignment shift is exactly what the cited single-axis studies are not structured to do.
defect_class: (b) universal negative about prior work, with (e) attribution mismatch
cited: No citation attached to the sentence; "the cited single-axis studies" is not enumerated.
why_unsupported: This asserts a capability gap across an unenumerated set of prior studies, and it is in tension with the same section's own characterisation of Hong et al. [37], which is described two paragraphs earlier as working "across a broader trust taxonomy" and which reports benign task performance alongside trust dimensions — i.e. it is not single-axis. As written the claim both over-generalises and mislabels at least one work the chapter itself cites.
proposed_fix: "Studies that report a single non-refusal or ASR axis without a paired capability anchor cannot separate these cases from a genuine alignment shift; that separation is what the matched-pair design adds here." (Name the specific studies meant, and exclude [37], which reports a capability axis.)

sentence: First, baseline safety profiles differ substantially between families even at matched factual capability, so calibration is a property of the release rather than of model size.
defect_class: (d) causal attribution to factors the study did not measure
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: The study measured fp16 baselines for one model per family (plus two Qwen sizes). Observing that baselines differ across families licenses no conclusion about *what* determines calibration. "A property of the release" attributes calibration to training/alignment recipe, which the study never varied or measured, and "rather than of model size" is directly contradicted by the report's own within-Qwen claim that scaling 1.7B->4B lowered baseline ASR by 14.0 pp (line 499) and by the fact that model size is confounded with release in every pair.
proposed_fix: "First, baseline safety profiles differ substantially between families even at matched factual capability. This study does not vary training or alignment recipe and so cannot say which release-level factor drives that difference."

sentence: This points the same direction as the broader literature on quantization sensitivity declining with model size.
defect_class: (e) attribution mismatch / uncited appeal to a body of literature
cited: No citation attached; no reference number appears in or near this sentence.
why_unsupported: An empirical claim about what "the broader literature" shows, with nothing cited.
